units.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
units.lo:
The observable properties of solids and liquids
How heating and cooling can change the state of materials
How scientific thinking helps us solve everyday problems

builtFrom.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of solids and liquids; How heating and cooling change state; Scientific thinking helps solve everyday problems

s.d: Can a computer tell a solid from a liquid just by looking? Open Teachable Machine in a browser on the front screen (or an iPad mirrored to the board) and use the iPad camera, keeping faces out of view, to collect photo examples of solids and liquids in clear containers for two labelled groups. Train the model, then test tricky items like water and a clear plastic block and compare its guesses with what students notice about shape and pouring.
s.why: A classifier's mistakes give students a useful reason to test materials rather than judge them only by appearance.

diff.support: Provide solid and liquid picture cards with a spoken starter: I would test it by...
diff.stretch: Test whether changing the background affects predictions, then explain why this is not evidence about the material.

s.quote: Comparing the properties of solids and liquids.
s.link: This turns the planned comparison of properties into a test of which observations actually help students distinguish solids from liquids.

s.d: An ice cube can seem unchanged until suddenly there is a puddle. Pairs share an iPad with Stop Motion Studio open and keep it still beside a shallow tray. Students photograph an ice cube at regular intervals while observing it directly between photographs. Play the frames quickly, then pause to locate the first visible liquid and the last remaining solid. Students check their original predictions against the replay and identify where solid ice and liquid water existed together.
s.why: Speeding up a real melting sequence makes gradual changes visible enough for students to inspect and discuss.

diff.support: Mark the device and tray positions with tape, and provide a simple photograph-taking role card.
diff.stretch: Compare equal ice cubes on two different surfaces, keeping the room, photograph intervals and starting size the same.

s.quote: Carefully watching experiments and changes in materials.
s.link: The replay extends the planned close observation of changes that can be easy to miss during an experiment.

s.d: Bring the class melting results together in one Microsoft Excel sheet on the front screen. Groups test equal-sized ice cubes in two classroom locations, using the same trays and recording minutes until no solid remains. The teacher enters each group's measurements and creates a column chart with a separate column for every result. Students compare repeated tests, spot unusual results and discuss differences in the testing conditions. Finish by checking whether the chart supports the class prediction about which location would melt ice faster.
s.why: A live class chart makes repeated results and unusual measurements easier to compare than separate group records.

diff.support: Give each group a recording strip with a start box, finish box and minutes box.
diff.stretch: Compare the spread of results within each location and suggest one change that could make a repeat test fairer.

s.quote: Using tables, drawings or diagrams to represent melting or freezing.
s.link: This builds on recording melting data by helping students compare results across the whole class.

s.d: Could the puddle become an ice cube again? Students open FlipaClip on their iPads and draw a short sequence showing ice melting, then water freezing in a freezer. They add arrows and labels showing when the surroundings warm or cool the water. Students play the sequence and check with a partner whether the water stays present throughout, rather than disappearing between states. Finish with a spoken explanation of why cooling can reverse this change, but simply pouring water into a cube-shaped container cannot.
s.why: Students can run a drawn change forwards and backwards to test whether their explanation includes both melting and freezing.

diff.support: Provide a four-box paper plan showing ice, melting ice, water and freezing water before students animate.
diff.stretch: Add a second sequence showing that liquid water changes shape in a new container without becoming a solid.

s.quote: How heating and cooling can change the state of materials (change, causation)…
s.link: This extends the heating and cooling inquiry by asking students to connect melting with its reverse change.

s.d: Return to the class's early predictions about solids and liquids. Each student opens Book Creator on their iPad and records their original claim as a short audio clip. They add photographs from their investigations and record a second explanation pointing to evidence about shape and flow. Students listen to both recordings in order and check whether their new claim matches the photographed observations. Finish by testing a mystery material, such as a wooden bead, so the teacher can hear students apply properties rather than guess from appearance.
s.why: Hearing an earlier prediction beside recorded evidence makes a change in understanding clear to both students and the teacher.

diff.support: Offer two spoken starters: At first I thought..., and Our test showed... because...
diff.stretch: Add a counter-example that challenges the claim that everything which pours must be a liquid.

s.quote: Considering how their thinking has changed through observations and experiments.
s.link: The paired recordings make the planner's reflection on changed thinking audible and grounded in experimental evidence.

s.d: How could we stop a chocolate decoration losing its shape before it is served? Groups compare equal chocolate pieces in sealed containers in a cooler spot and a warmer spot, observing without tasting. Students then open Adobe Express on their iPads to assemble a short video using photographs and recorded narration from the test. They show the comparison and give storage advice that follows their evidence. Finish by presenting the proposed fix and explaining how reducing warming helps the chocolate remain solid.
s.why: A short evidence-based video lets students replay a practical solution and show exactly how it uses cooling.

diff.support: Provide three filming prompts: show the problem, show the test, show the advice.
diff.stretch: Test the advice with a different amount of chocolate and explain whether the original recommendation still holds.

s.quote: Using knowledge of changes of state to explain real-life examples (e.g. melting chocolate, freezing water).
s.link: Students use their changes-of-state observations to give and justify practical advice about an everyday melting problem.

stem.d: With 15 minutes of prep, set out small recycled containers, cardboard, foil, fabric scraps, tape, sealed ice packs and two Micro:bits loaded with a simple temperature display. Groups build an insulated cool box and compare it with a plain matching container at a test station, keeping the boards dry and away from the ice packs. Students improve one part of their insulation and test again to see if it kept the inside cooler.
stem.why: Temperature readings help students compare their handmade containers and choose an improvement using evidence rather than appearance.

diff.support: Provide matching containers and a simple results table, with clear builder, reader and recorder roles.
diff.stretch: Repeat the test using the same total amount of insulation arranged differently, then compare the temperature changes.

stem.quote: How scientific thinking helps us solve everyday problems (responsibility)…
stem.link: Students use a fair comparison and measured evidence to improve a practical design for keeping materials cool.

units.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
units.lo:
The ways people use technology to express their creativity.
How texts and images work together.
How technology influences our creativity.

builtFrom.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
builtFrom.lo: The ways people use technology to express creativity; How texts and images work together; How technology influences our creativity

s.d: Can the same drawing suggest a peaceful world and a noisy one? Students open Brushes Redux on their iPads and draw the same familiar place twice, once to feel peaceful and once to feel noisy. They explore brush size and colour, using undo to compare choices before committing. Allow one lesson, with five minutes beforehand to check the drawing tools. Finish by showing examples and asking students to identify which digital choices suggest peace or noise, revealing whether they connect artistic choices with meaning.
s.why: Quickly undoing and comparing marks helps students notice how digital tools influence their creative choices.

diff.support: Give students three drawing choices to explore: thin lines, thick lines and contrasting colours.
diff.stretch: Create a counter-example where adding more digital effects makes the intended meaning harder to recognise.

s.quote: As they experiment with these digital mediums, students will become familiar with the artistic potential each app offers, discovering how technology can support their visual expression, enhance their ideas, and open new pathways for making art.
s.link: This begins the visual art exploration by making the influence of drawing tools visible.

s.d: Students open Book Creator on their iPads, photograph a small arrangement of classroom objects, and add a caption that gives the photo a surprising twist. They record themselves reading the caption with expression, then show a partner the photo first before revealing the words and audio. Listeners explain which clue changed how they read the picture.
s.why: Revealing an image, caption and recorded voice separately lets students test how each changes a reader's understanding.

diff.support: Offer the caption starter, 'At first this looks like..., but...', for students to complete orally.
diff.stretch: Add a deliberately conflicting narration and test which source of meaning listeners trust most.

s.quote: How texts and images work together.
s.link: This turns the text and image inquiry into a practical investigation of how meaning changes.

s.d: Bring back the picture book image from Music and pick two details to turn into sounds. Students open GarageBand on their iPads, choose an instrument for each detail and record two short parts using notes from their pentatonic scale. Play selected tracks in a listening circle so classmates can guess which part of the picture each sound represents.
s.why: Recording and replaying separate musical parts lets students hear how sounds combine to represent features of an image.

diff.support: Give each student two image features to represent and a choice of two instrument sounds.
diff.stretch: Keep the notes unchanged but alter tempo to test whether the image suggests a different kind of movement.

s.quote: Music: students worked in small groups to create a composition inspired by a picture book image.
s.link: This extends the existing music composition by letting students isolate and compare the contribution of each part.

s.d: Pairs use an iPad in Stop Motion Studio and build a paper face with movable eyebrows and mouth. Keeping the camera steady, they take step-by-step photos to animate a neutral face turning surprised. Pairs replay their clip, adjust any jumpy frames, and share it so classmates can spot the first clue that shows the feeling.
s.why: Frame-by-frame playback makes tiny changes in an expression visible and lets students control how quickly a feeling emerges.

diff.support: Provide a paper face with separate eyebrows and mouth, plus a six-photo planning strip.
diff.stretch: Keep the final expression identical but change the transition speed to test whether viewers interpret the feeling differently.

s.quote: Facial expression as a form of communication Term 1 - students explore how we communicate and express ourselves using our faces.
s.link: This extends the drama exploration by letting students slow down and inspect the movements that communicate feelings.

s.d: The same closed box can feel ordinary or mysterious depending on the edit. Pairs share an iPad with iMovie to film three short shots of a hand approaching and opening a box, then edit a quick version and a slower version that holds before the reveal. Screen both edits so students can compare how timing builds tension.
s.why: Editing the same footage in two ways lets students test how timing shapes an audience's sense of tension.

diff.support: Provide a three-shot plan: closed box, approaching hand, opened box.
diff.stretch: Keep shot lengths fixed and test whether changing only their order alters what viewers expect.

s.quote: They also learn to analyse dramatic tension through in film and television and how/why certain elements are used.
s.link: This makes the drama study of film tension testable through students' own editing decisions.

s.d: Each student opens their own Seesaw portfolio on their iPad and photographs their finished artwork. Using the drawing and voice tools, they circle and explain two choices they made to express their view of the world. Classmates listen to a partner's post and leave a short spoken comment about one idea that stood out.
s.why: Recorded voice and drawing let students point out creative decisions that may not be obvious in the finished artwork.

diff.support: Offer the spoken starter, 'I wanted to show..., so I chose...', on a small desk card beside their iPad.
diff.stretch: Identify a creative choice that did not work and explain when that same choice might suit another message.

s.quote: Student self-assessment and peer feedback…
s.link: This gives students a practical way to explain their creative decisions and respond to classmates' work.

stem.t: Cardboard Faces That Change Their Minds
stem.d: Allow 15 minutes to gather cardboard, tape, fabric scraps and Micro:bits. Pairs build a cardboard face with a window for the Micro:bit LED grid, then connect a Micro:bit to an iPad in MakeCode so button A and button B show two different eye expressions. They test both faces with classmates and adjust one detail so each feeling reads clearly.
stem.why: A programmable display lets students test how changing just the eyes alters the message of a physical face.

diff.support: Provide a cardboard face outline and a printed five-by-five grid for planning two eye patterns.
diff.stretch: Add a third expression triggered by pressing both buttons, then test whether viewers can distinguish all three.

stem.quote: They look into the universal facial expressions and further build their understanding on reading expressions and changing expressions to communicate feelings in various situations…
stem.link: This builds on the drama exploration by combining a handmade face with programmable changes that classmates can interpret.

units.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

builtFrom.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

s.d: Pairs pick from four classroom invention ideas, such as a quieter chair foot or an automatic pencil sorter, and decide whether each is a need or a want. The teacher enters the class votes into one Microsoft Excel sheet on the front screen to build a live column chart. Watch how the chart shifts if students re-vote after hearing other reasons.
s.why: A live chart makes differences in students' priorities visible and gives them evidence to discuss why inventions appeal to different people.

diff.support: Provide four pictured inventions and the spoken starter, 'This meets a need because...'
diff.stretch: Compare choices for two different settings and explain why the same invention might move between need and want.

s.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
s.link: This gives the planner's opening question a concrete classroom problem and makes students' starting ideas visible.

s.d: Students open Popplet on their iPads and photograph everyday tech around the classroom, such as a screen, keyboard, speaker or iPad. They connect each photo to a short label explaining what job that part does. Pairs then compare mind maps and move or relink bubbles as they talk through how the parts work together as one system.
s.why: Movable pictures and connecting lines help students revise their thinking about how computer parts work together rather than simply naming them.

diff.support: Give students four classroom items to photograph and the starter, 'This part helps us...'
diff.stretch: Add a component that can both receive and send information, and explain why it needs two connections.

s.quote: Create a mind map in Popplet app…
s.link: This develops the planned systems picture sort into a revisable map of components and their functions.

s.d: Students open FlipaClip on their iPads and draw two devices linked by a network connection. Across six short frames, they animate a coloured message travelling from the sender, along the connection, to the receiver. Students record a brief voice note explaining why the signal needs a real path between devices rather than floating through empty space.
s.why: Animation makes an invisible journey visible, so students can replay and correct their explanation of how connected devices exchange information.

diff.support: Provide a paper sketch showing a sending device, network equipment and receiving device to copy into the animation.
diff.stretch: Animate a second version with a broken connection and show where the message can no longer travel.

s.quote: What happens inside our computers and networks when we send a message or a picture to someone else?
s.link: This answers the planner's network question by giving students a moving model they can inspect and explain.

s.d: Students build a simple floor map of the school using paper labels for key spots like the library, classrooms and oval. In small groups with a Sphero BOLT and an iPad running the Sphero Edu app, they code the robot to travel from one landmark to another using roll and heading blocks. When the robot veers off course, groups tweak one block at a time until it reaches the target.
s.why: A moving robot gives immediate evidence of whether a sequence works, making testing and debugging purposeful rather than imaginary.

diff.support: Mark the starting position and provide a paper plan with just two straight sections and one turn.
diff.stretch: Change the starting direction and adjust the program while keeping the same destination and avoiding the same obstacles.

s.quote: Elaborations: creating a two-dimensional plan of the school on a floor mat, representing key buildings and landmarks, then programming a robot to move to different locations within the space.
s.link: This directly develops the planned school map and robot task into a test of commands, sequences and debugging.

s.d: Each student opens their own Seesaw portfolio on their iPad and photographs a fictional message card asking for a password, photo or address. They record spoken advice explaining the risk and what to do next, such as stopping and checking with a trusted adult. Students listen back and re-record if their advice left out a clear safe action.
s.why: Listening back to a recorded explanation helps students notice whether their safety advice gives a clear action and a reason.

diff.support: Offer the spoken structure, 'I notice... I would... because...', alongside two pictured fictional situations.
diff.stretch: Explain how a seemingly friendly message could still ask for private information, and identify a safe next step.

s.quote: Library: In Library, students explored the theme of digital wellbeing and citizenship through stories about balancing screen time, safe internet use, and responsible online behavior.
s.link: This revisits the Library safety work and captures students' final reasoning about privacy and responsible choices.

s.d: Spend 10 minutes setting up one class Microsoft Form in a web browser with a short branching scenario based on students' online-safety rules. Pairs help draft two possible responses and consequences for the class form, then students open the published link on their iPads to test both routes without entering names. Discuss why the safer choice protects everyone.
s.why: Branching choices let students test how different online decisions lead to different consequences within a safe fictional situation.

diff.support: Provide two ready-written choices so pairs can concentrate on explaining the consequence of each action.
diff.stretch: Add a third route where a student repairs an unkind choice and explain why deleting alone may not repair harm.

s.quote: How can we be safe, kind, and fair digital citizens when we use online spaces?
s.link: Students turn the planner's citizenship question into a working decision activity that classmates can test.

stem.d: Allow 15 minutes to gather cardboard, fabric scraps, tape and popsticks, and load each Micro:bit with a simple light-reading display. Groups of four build a model window frame with an adjustable shade and record three Micro:bit readings with the shade open and closed. They adjust one part of the shade and test again to see if it cuts more glare.
stem.why: Light readings give students evidence to compare shade designs and decide whether a physical change actually blocks more light.

diff.support: Provide a folded cardboard frame and assign builder, sensor reader, recorder and tester roles within each group.
diff.stretch: Test the improved shade with light coming from a second direction and redesign it to work in both positions.

stem.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
stem.link: This turns the planner's design question into a physical invention that students can measure, improve and justify.

units.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
units.lo:
Soils, rocks, and minerals have observable properties that make them useful in different ways.
Earth's resources are vital for living things, including humans, and must be used responsibly.
First Nations Australians have long-standing knowledge and cultural uses of soils, rocks, and minerals.

builtFrom.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals; Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly; First Nations knowledge of soils and rocks

s.d: What can a school-ground rock reveal when we look around it rather than just at its front? With five minutes of preparation, choose an accessible, textured rock beside a safe walking space. Students open the Scaniverse app on their iPads and move slowly around it to create their own 3D scan. Back inside, they rotate and enlarge their model with a partner to check observations about texture, cracks and its use in the grounds. Finish with a spoken before-and-after claim that distinguishes an observed property from a guess about the rock's identity.
s.why: A rotatable scan lets students revisit a large rock indoors and check their first observations from different angles.

diff.support: Give students three observation prompts: colour, surface texture and how the rock is being used.
diff.stretch: Find a feature the scan misses and explain why examining the real rock still matters.

s.quote: Geology quest: identify examples of rocks and soil in the school grounds and record how they are being used.
s.link: This extends the geology quest by giving students a rock model they can revisit when checking their observations.

s.d: Does a shaken soil sample settle all at once? Prepare sealed clear jars containing soil and water in about ten minutes. Pairs share an iPad, record a stationary video of their shaken jar settling, then open the clip in the IMovie app. Students trim the waiting time and increase playback speed to reveal particles settling at different rates. They record a short explanation over the clip, using their magnifying-glass observations as evidence. Replay the films to check predictions about whether every soil component behaves the same way.
s.why: Speeding up a recording reveals settling patterns that are easy to miss while watching soil and water separate.

diff.support: Provide a simple spoken sentence starter: First we noticed, then we noticed, so we think.
diff.stretch: Repeat with a different soil sample while keeping water volume and recording time the same.

s.quote: Using magnifying glasses, they identify components (pebbles, sand, plant matter, insects).
s.link: This adds a moving record to the local soil study so students can investigate how a mixture separates.

s.d: Choose two coastal places beforehand, one in Australia and one in Indonesia. Students open the Google Maps app on their iPads (no sign-in needed) and explore Street View scenes to spot rock, plants, farms and buildings. Working alongside a partner, they sort what they can see into a paper Venn diagram and note one question they would need another source to answer.
s.why: Changing scale and viewing actual landscapes helps students connect visible land use with the natural features they are comparing.

diff.support: Give students a paper comparison sheet with spaces for visible land, plants, buildings and questions.
diff.stretch: Inspect a second location in each country and identify evidence that challenges the first comparison.

s.quote: Comparison: Students create a Venn diagram or report comparing natural features of Australia with a neighbouring country.
s.link: This gives the planned comparison a shared base of visible landscape evidence before students make broader claims.

s.d: After exploring a class First Nations resource about ochre, stone or clay, students open Book Creator on their iPads to make one short page. They add a photo or drawing of the natural material, label how it is used, and record a short voice note explaining why that knowledge matters and acknowledging whose knowledge it is. Share a few pages together to discuss both practical uses and cultural value.
s.why: Pairing images with a recorded voice note lets students explain First Nations uses of natural materials carefully in their own words.

diff.support: Provide three clear prompts for the voice note: the material, how it is used, and why it is valued.
diff.stretch: Add a second voice note naming one question you would still like to learn from a First Nations source.

s.quote: Cultural Knowledge: Students explain how First Nations Australians use a particular rock, mineral, or soil resource and reflect on its value.
s.link: This gives students a clear, respectful way to record what they learn from class First Nations resources about ochre, stone or soil.

s.d: Students open Minecraft Education on their iPads and start a new world in Creative mode. They build a small cutaway landscape showing soil, rock, plants and a spot where people gather a natural resource, with a path classmates can walk through. Each student then changes one design choice to protect soil or plants and explains the trade-off to a partner.
s.why: An explorable model makes students show how resource use affects nearby living things, rather than simply listing useful materials.

diff.support: Provide a paper cross-section sketch showing a soil layer, rock layer, plants and one access route.
diff.stretch: Add a competing land use and redesign the model to explain a trade-off rather than an easy solution.

s.quote: How do soils, rocks, and minerals connect living things and societies across places?
s.link: This turns the concluding presentation into an explorable explanation of resource use and its effects on living things.

s.d: Students open the Canva app on their iPads to turn their school-ground observations into a short 30-second video about one small way to protect soil, such as sticking to paths. They record a quick clip and voiceover showing the spot, the problem and their suggested action. Play a few clips for the class before testing the action outside.
s.why: A short demonstration with narration makes a practical soil-care action easier for the class to follow and repeat.

diff.support: Give students a three-part spoken script: the problem, our action and how it protects soil.
diff.stretch: Add a close-up comparison showing when the proposed action would not be enough to prevent damage.

s.quote: Earth's resources are vital for living things, including humans, and must be used responsibly.
s.link: This develops the responsibility line of inquiry into a manageable action based on the geology quest's school-ground observations.

stem.d: Allow 10 minutes to gather cardboard, popsticks, tape and recycled containers. Groups of four build a low bridge over a paper garden bed, then share a Sphero BOLT and an iPad to code a slow, straight crossing from the same start point. When the bridge sags or a wheel slips, groups strengthen one part and run three steady crossings.
stem.why: A programmed robot provides a repeatable moving load, helping students test and improve a bridge that protects the model soil below.

diff.support: Provide two equal-height supports and a straight route so groups can focus on strengthening the bridge deck.
diff.stretch: Keep the same bridge span but reduce the amount of cardboard while maintaining three successful crossings.

stem.quote: Earth's resources are vital for living things, including humans, and must be used responsibly.
stem.link: This makes responsible resource use tangible by challenging students to preserve access while protecting a model growing area.

units.th: Where We Are in Place and Time
units.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
units.lo:
How Australia and its neighbouring regions define places
First Nations Australians have deep and ongoing connections to Country, which are spiritual, cultural, and environmental.
Places can be understood and valued in different ways, depending on cultural and historical perspectives.

builtFrom.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
builtFrom.lo: How Australia and neighbouring regions define places; Australia's states/territories have unique identities; First Nations connections to Country

s.d: Students open a teacher-prepared board in the Padlet app on their iPads. Each student photographs a favourite school spot (with no people in frame), posts it to the class board and records a short voice note explaining why that place matters to them. Back inside, play contrasting clips beside the photos to see how different people experience the same place.
s.why: Hearing different students describe the same photograph makes contrasting views of a familiar place easy to notice.

diff.support: Offer the spoken starter, 'This place matters to me because', beside three teacher-taken school photographs.
diff.stretch: Find two recordings that disagree about a place and suggest why both views might make sense.

s.quote: Students can find a favourite place in the JS to capture, paint or sketch.
s.link: This adds students' spoken perspectives to the planner's exploration of meaningful school places.

s.d: Students open the Google Maps app on their iPads (no sign-in needed) after predicting compass directions from Australia to Indonesia and New Zealand. They zoom out to check directions, then drop into Street View in both countries to sketch one real detail beside each label. Compare their sketches to see what street-level views show that flat map symbols hide.
s.why: Moving between a regional map and street-level views connects compass directions with visible details of real places.

diff.support: Provide a compass card and two named destinations for students to locate together.
diff.stretch: Compare a coastal and inland location in the same neighbouring country and explain a difference visible on screen.

s.quote: How can we use maps to learn about Aust and our neighbouring countries?
s.link: This builds on locating Australia's neighbours and revising compass directions.

s.d: Using stories and resources shared in class about First Nations connections to Country, students open Popplet on their iPads to sort ideas into three colour-coded groups: caring for land, belonging, and living culture today. They link examples that fit more than one group, then compare maps with a partner to explain why Country means much more than a place on a map.
s.why: Colour-coded bubbles help students see how spiritual, cultural and environmental connections to Country overlap rather than sitting in separate boxes.

diff.support: Start with the three group headings already placed in Popplet so students can focus on adding examples.
diff.stretch: Draw linking lines between examples that belong in two groups and explain the connection aloud.

s.quote: What connections do First Australians have to Country and Place?
s.link: This helps students organise what they learn from class First Nations resources around the planner's question about Country and Place.

s.d: Students open Minecraft Education on their iPads and start a flat world in Creative mode to model a small coastal dune area. They build a visitor path and lookout that keeps people off the fragile plants, then walk the route in first-person view to spot and block tempting shortcuts. Pairs share a quick walkthrough explaining how their design protects the area.
s.why: Walking through a model reveals whether a proposed visitor route actually protects the feature students want people to respect.

diff.support: Provide a small building area and a paper checklist showing entrance, path and protected feature.
diff.stretch: Test whether two visitors travelling in opposite directions can pass without leaving the path, then improve the design.

s.quote: Choose a place or feature of Australia and write and how and why people could show respect for it.
s.link: This lets students test a practical way visitors could show respect before explaining their design choices.

s.d: Students open National Geographic MapMaker in a web browser on their iPads beside their original world maps. After predicting which countries sit closest to Australia, they zoom out to locate them and zoom in to compare coastlines against country borders. Students add corrections to their paper maps in a new colour and share one surprise with a partner.
s.activity: Add new learning to world map
s.why: Live zooming lets students test their original map ideas against geographic detail that appears at different scales.

diff.support: Give students a short checklist: find Australia, trace its coastline, then locate one neighbouring country.
diff.stretch: Find a neighbouring country spread across several islands and explain why separate land areas do not always mean separate countries.

s.quote: Students are given their original world map and asked to add to it - using a different colour to show new learning.
s.link: This adds a live map investigation to the concluding assessment, so students test their earlier ideas before marking new learning.

s.d: Invite students to pick a place they have visited, including somewhere close to home. In GarageBand on their iPads, they record two short voice clips on separate tracks: one describing what they noticed there, and one explaining why that place mattered to them. Students trim long pauses, play selected recordings for the class, and agree on one simple way to care for a similar local place.
s.why: Combining contrasting spoken memories lets the class hear how different experiences shape what students notice and value.

diff.support: Provide the sentence frame, 'I noticed..., and this mattered to me because...', for each recording.
diff.stretch: Record a contrasting interpretation of the same observed feature and explain how both interpretations could be reasonable.

s.quote: Taking Action Students come back from their holiday and talk about where they went and what they noticed.
s.link: This turns the holiday discussion into a comparison of valued places and a realistic local action.

stem.d: Allow 10 minutes to gather cardboard, fabric scraps, popsticks and tape, and set out Sphero BOLT robots with their control iPads. Groups of four build a tabletop dune route on the floor using fabric for plants and cardboard for barriers, then code BOLT along the path. When it clips a barrier, groups tweak a bend and test three clean runs.
stem.why: A moving robot exposes tight corners and unreliable routes, giving students clear evidence for improving their physical visitor-path designs.

diff.support: Provide a taped start and finish, with a simple command sequence students can adjust.
diff.stretch: Reduce the path width while keeping three successful runs, then explain the trade-off between access and protected space.

stem.quote: Choose a place or feature of Australia and write and how and why people could show respect for it.
stem.link: This makes showing respect for an Australian landscape a practical build, test and improve task.

units.ci: Strategies support healthy relationships and personal growth.
units.lo:
How our words, actions and choices affect others
Ways we can solve problems and manage conflict respectfully
Why is it important to listen to feedback and use it to grow
What helps us keep going when things get tricky

builtFrom.ci: The choices and actions we make contribute to our health and wellbeing.
builtFrom.lo: What it means to be healthy; Choices and their impact on health; Actions to maintain a healthy mind and body

s.d: Can the same friendly action feel different to two people? Before class, spend ten minutes making three fictional school scenarios in Microsoft Forms in a web browser. Students open the form in a web browser on their iPads and choose how someone might feel in each scenario. Show the anonymous response charts on the front screen and invite students to explain the differences. Revisit the most divided response to hear whether students recognise that good intentions do not always match another person's experience.
s.why: An instant class chart reveals different interpretations of the same action and gives students a reason to listen.

diff.support: Read each scenario aloud and offer the sentence starter, "Someone might feel this way because..."
diff.stretch: Suggest one missing detail that could change how students interpret the same action.

s.quote: Goal: To identify and describe friendly behaviour at school.
s.link: This builds on the friendly behaviour provocation by making different interpretations visible before the class agrees on helpful actions.

s.d: What changes when "You can join us" sounds welcoming in one recording and annoyed in another? Set up one shared recording station with the Podcast Equipment while groups rehearse away from screens. Each group records the same fictional invitation twice, changing only tone, pace or emphasis. Play the recordings to the class without identifying the intended feeling, and collect listeners' interpretations. Finish by recording a class explanation of how delivery can make friendly words feel unfriendly.
s.why: Recorded voices let students replay and compare how tone changes the meaning of exactly the same words.

diff.support: Provide two short scripts with the same words and mark where speakers should pause.
diff.stretch: Record a third version where tone and words disagree, then ask listeners which message they trust.

s.quote: How our words, actions and choices affect others…
s.link: This extends the planner's exploration of unfriendly behaviour by separating the words spoken from the way they sound.

s.d: After discussing the friendship scenarios, students open Popplet on their iPads. They create bubbles for three fictional disagreements and add connected bubbles showing possible respectful responses. Students move and reconnect ideas as they decide which strategies suit more than one situation. Show two maps on the front screen and discuss where a calming strategy needs to come before talking. Finish with an unfamiliar scenario so students can explain why solving conflict is not simply saying sorry straight away.
s.why: Movable, connected ideas help students compare which strategies fit different conflicts rather than treating every disagreement the same way.

diff.support: Offer three strategy cards with simple pictures for students to copy into their map.
diff.stretch: Add a situation where a usually helpful strategy is unsuitable, and explain a better first step.

s.quote: Ways we can solve problems and manage conflict respectfully…
s.link: This helps students organise the planner's conflict and emotional regulation strategies into choices they can explain.

s.d: Give each pair a Micro:bit to connect to an iPad with the MakeCode editor open in a web browser. In two lessons, students code button A to show a friendly face and button B to show a different image. A nearby pair tests both buttons and gives one specific piece of feedback about whether the images are recognisable. Students set one small goal, change their code and test again, keeping a brief spoken account of any failed attempt. Finish by demonstrating a working fix and naming the strategy that helped them keep going.
s.why: A working program gives immediate evidence that a small change and another attempt can turn useful feedback into progress.

diff.support: Provide a picture of the two button-event blocks and assign separate coder and tester roles.
diff.stretch: Make both buttons together show a third image, then test whether the original two controls still work.

s.quote: What helps us keep going when things get tricky…
s.link: This gives the planner's work on persistence and goal setting a small, testable challenge with visible results.

s.d: Students open the Canva app on their iPads to build a Colour, Symbol, Image page for the unit. They pick a background colour, a simple icon and an image that show what they have learned about healthy friendships, then add a short caption or voice note explaining each choice. Pairs swap iPads to see if their partner can read the message in their choices.
s.why: Keeping an original beside a revised explanation makes the effect of specific feedback visible and easy to discuss.

diff.support: Offer three friendship strategies to choose from and the starter, 'I chose this symbol because...'
diff.stretch: Add one extra note explaining how your symbol or colour would change during a tricky disagreement.

s.d: Students open the Adobe Express app on their iPads to turn their Friendship Fire graphic novel into a short three-scene narrated comic. Using drawings or supplied images, they add speech bubbles for what characters say aloud and record voiceovers for what the other character is thinking. Small groups watch each comic and point out the respectful strategy that helped repair the friendship.
s.why: Recorded character thoughts reveal the difference between what someone says aloud and what they may be feeling inside.

diff.support: Provide a three-panel paper plan labelled disagreement, respectful response and next step before students open the tool.
diff.stretch: Add a character whose first assumption is wrong, then reveal the evidence that changes their response.

s.quote: Create a graphic novel that features a Friendship Fire.
s.link: This develops the planned graphic novel by making both spoken words and hidden perspectives available for classmates to compare.

stem.d: Allow 10 minutes to gather cardboard, tape, straws and popsticks, and mark a short floor route with a wide turn. Groups of four build a lightweight chariot carrying a paper passenger for Sphero BOLT to pull, using a shared control iPad at one steady speed. After each run, groups fix one weak spot and test again to show how feedback improved the build.
stem.why: A repeatable robot journey lets students compare design changes fairly and see whether their team's feedback improved the build.

diff.support: Provide a simple folded-card chassis example and assign builder, driver, observer and recorder roles.
diff.stretch: Test whether the improved chariot still carries its load around a tighter turn without changing the driving speed.

stem.quote: Sphero challenge task, Friendship Fire story writing and our Sphero Chariot race.
stem.link: This extends the planner's chariot task into a build-test-improve challenge where students can demonstrate listening, shared roles and persistence.
